subject: English
source: Drive English KS3 3yr Scheme of Work (Autobiography unit: Boy, Roald Dahl; Year 7 Autumn 1) adapted, with AQA GCSE Language assessment-objective alignment; National Curriculum KS3 English. All model texts are teacher-written originals.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Life writing - autobiography and memoir
lessons.title: What is life writing? Autobiography, memoir and identity
objectives: Distinguish autobiography, biography, memoir and diary
Identify the typical features of autobiographical writing
Write a short first-person recount of a moment that shaped you

keywords.def: the story of a person's life written by that person
the story of a person's life written by someone else
a writer's account of particular memories or a period of their life
the qualities and roles that make a person who they are
writing from the ‘I’ viewpoint, using I, me and my

starter: Bismillah. Write down three nouns that describe your home or your school.
Which word class is the underlined word? ‘She walked slowly home.’
Write one sentence that uses the connective ‘because’.

teach.heading: Writing about a life
bullets: Biography: someone else writes your life
Autobiography: you write your own life
Memoir: you write about certain memories
Diary: you write day by day
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask: ‘Who has read a book about a real person?’ Take examples. Explain that these are all forms of life writing and that each has a different voice. Anne Frank's diary was written day by day while she was in hiding in Amsterdam in the 1940s; it is a diary, not an autobiography written looking back. Misconception: pupils think every true story is an autobiography. Check by asking who the writer is.

teach.heading: Why do people write about themselves?
bullets: To inform: tell readers what happened
To entertain: make readers laugh or gasp
To reflect: understand what an event meant
To inspire: show that change is possible
teach.note: Link purposes to audiences. An athlete's autobiography is for fans; a war survivor's memoir is for future generations. Ask: ‘If you wrote your life story, who would read it and why?’ Take three answers. Note that a text can have more than one purpose.

teach.heading: Features of autobiographical writing
bullets: First person: I, me, my, we
Past tense: ‘I remember…’, ‘we ran’
Mostly chronological order, with time markers
Thoughts and feelings, not just events
Reflection: what the writer learned
teach.note: Display the model extract on the next slide and ask pupils to find each feature. Key point: autobiography is not a list of events; the reflection is what makes it powerful. Misconception: that you must tell everything. Writers choose the moments that matter.

teach.heading: Model extract: spot the features
bullets: ‘I was nine when I rode off the end of the pier.’
Time marker: ‘that summer’, ‘for a moment’
Feeling: ‘my face burned’
Reflection: ‘I learned to laugh at myself’
teach.note: Teacher-written model to read aloud: ‘I was nine the summer I rode Uncle Idris's bicycle straight off the end of the jetty. For one long second the wheels spun in the air. Then came the cold slap of the water and a whole beach roaring with laughter. My face burned hotter than the sand. Looking back, I am glad they laughed, because it taught me that I could laugh too.’ Ask pupils to tell you the tense, the viewpoint, a feeling, and a reflection. Praise precise answers.

teach.heading: Identity: the many ‘me's
bullets: We are more than one thing: son, pupil, Muslim, friend
Writers choose which part of themselves to show
Our identity can change as we grow
teach.note: Pupils mind-map their identities (3 minutes, in chat or on a shared whiteboard). Stress that no one has to share anything private: right to pass. Discuss how a footballer's autobiography shows a different ‘self’ from the same person's school report. Link to the RECIPE value of Integrity: being honest about who we are.

practice: Sort into biography, autobiography, memoir or diary: (a) a book by Michelle Obama about her own life, Becoming; (b) an encyclopaedia entry on Marie Curie; (c) a girl's daily notes written in hiding in Amsterdam; (d) I Am Malala, Malala Yousafzai's account of her life, written with Christina Lamb.
Read the model extract again. Find the tense, one time marker and one feeling. Which sentence is the reflection?
Which TWO of these would you expect in an autobiography? ‘She was born in…’ / ‘I was terrified’ / ‘Next month the team will…’ / ‘I remember the smell of the bakery.’
independent: Write 5-6 sentences titled ‘A moment that made me who I am’. Use first person, past tense, and finish with one sentence of reflection.
Underline two time markers and one feeling word in your own writing.
Extension: rewrite your first sentence so it starts with a feeling or a sound instead of ‘I’.
exit: Name two differences between an autobiography and a biography.
Write one sentence of reflection beginning ‘Looking back, I realise…’.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member for five minutes about a childhood memory and write down four true facts about it, ready for next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a sentence-starter frame (‘I remember… I felt… I learned…’). EAL: pre-teach tense and viewpoint with picture cards. Stretch: compare the voice of the model extract with a published memoir extract chosen by the teacher.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Life writing - autobiography and memoir
lessons.title: Telling a life in order: chronology and consequential connectives
objectives: Use time adverbials and consequential connectives accurately
Vary sentence openings beyond subject-verb
Experiment with playing with chronology for effect

keywords.def: events told in the order they happened
a word or phrase that says when something happened, e.g. later that day
a word that shows result, e.g. so, therefore, as a result
a part of a text that jumps back to an earlier time
the form of a verb that shows when something happens

starter: Which features of an autobiography can you remember? Name three.
Is this a biography or an autobiography? ‘My grandmother taught me to bake.’
Put in order: ‘Finally… / First… / Then…’

teach.heading: Putting events in order
bullets: Chronological: first, next, then, finally
Time adverbials: that morning, an hour later
Time words guide the reader through the story
teach.note: Say bismillah. Model a weekend in chronological order using four time adverbials, then ask a pupil to retell theirs in 20 seconds using two. Ask: ‘Why does a reader need time markers?’ Misconception: pupils overuse ‘then’. Challenge them to find alternatives.

teach.heading: Showing cause and effect
bullets: so
therefore
as a result
consequently
because of this
teach.note: Explain consequential connectives show result: ‘The bus was late, so I missed the start.’ Model correct punctuation: ‘The bus was late; as a result, I missed the start’ or a full stop before a sentence starting ‘As a result,’. Ask pupils to complete: ‘I forgot my homework, therefore…’. Common error: comma splice before ‘therefore’.

teach.heading: Starting sentences in different ways
bullets: Subject-verb: ‘I ran to the gate.’
Time adverbial: ‘By noon, I was exhausted.’
-ing opener: ‘Gripping the rail, I stepped on.’
Connective: ‘Because it rained, we stayed in.’
teach.note: Show a paragraph where every sentence starts with ‘I’ and ask how it sounds. Then redraft together. The point: subject-verb openings are fine and clear, but varied openings keep the reader interested. Do not ask for every sentence to differ: control, not decoration.

teach.heading: Playing with time
bullets: Start at the end, then flash back
Use ‘Months earlier…’ to move back in time
Return to the present for the reflection
teach.note: Model an opening: ‘The trophy still sits on my shelf, slightly crooked. It was not always so proud.’ Then flash back. Explain that skilled writers sometimes break chronology to create interest, but must signal the shift clearly with a time adverbial. Ask: ‘What mistake could confuse a reader?’ (changing tense without warning).

practice: Combine using a consequential connective: ‘The alarm did not ring. I woke late.’ Then write a second version with a time adverbial at the start.
Rewrite so only two sentences begin with ‘I’: ‘I woke up. I ate breakfast. I packed my bag. I ran for the bus. I sat down. I felt relieved.’
Spot the error: ‘It rained heavily, therefore we stayed inside all day.’ Correct the punctuation.
independent: Write a weekend recount of 6 sentences in chronological order, using at least three different time adverbials and two consequential connectives.
Rewrite your recount starting with the END of the weekend, then flash back. Signal the shift clearly.
Extension: use one -ing opener and one ‘because’ opener, underlining each.
exit: Write a sentence using ‘as a result’ correctly.
Write a sentence that opens with a time adverbial.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph about last Friday that begins with the end of the day and uses at least four time adverbials.
lessons.send: SEND: give a connective bank on cards and a sequencing grid. EAL: allow oral rehearsal before writing. Stretch: insert one flashback and one forward-looking sentence.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Voice, humour and description (Roald Dahl's Boy)
lessons.title: Meet Roald Dahl: Boy, the preface and sentence types
objectives: Learn about Roald Dahl and the book Boy: Tales of Childhood
Identify and use the four sentence types for effect
Write a short preface for your own life story

keywords.def: an introduction at the start of a book explaining its purpose
a sentence that tells something
a sentence that asks, ending in a question mark
a sentence that gives an order or instruction
a sentence that shows strong feeling, ending in !

starter: Rewrite with a connective: ‘It was cold. We wore coats.’
Name two time adverbials.
Why might a writer start with the end of a story?

teach.heading: The writer: Roald Dahl
bullets: Born in Llandaff, Cardiff, in 1916
Norwegian parents; famous children's author
Boy: Tales of Childhood published in 1984
Died in 1990
teach.note: Ask what pupils know of Dahl (Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda, The BFG). Explain that Boy is not a complete life story; it is a collection of memorable episodes from his childhood, told with humour. Say bismillah and keep the tone light but focused. Check facts against the class copy of the book.

teach.heading: What is a preface for?
bullets: Tells readers what the book is and is not
Sets the tone and the voice
Speaks directly to the reader
Gives a reason to keep reading
teach.note: Read the opening pages of Boy from the school copy or the Roald Dahl website. Do not reproduce the text on slides. Ask: ‘How does Dahl talk to you? Does he sound like a teacher or a friend?’ Note that he explains he is not writing a complete history of himself, only the things he remembers. Link to autobiography versus memoir from lesson 1.

teach.heading: Four sentence types
bullets: Statement: ‘I remember the sweet shop.’
Question: ‘Have you ever been so afraid you froze?’
Command: ‘Imagine the smell of burnt toast.’
Exclamation: ‘What a morning that was!’
teach.note: Practise identifying types quickly: say a sentence, pupils hold up 1-4 fingers. Explain a question mark does not always make a question (rhetorical questions) and a command may have no exclamation mark. Misconception: that every exclamation is a shout; the key is strong feeling.

teach.heading: Why mix sentence types?
bullets: Questions pull the reader in
Commands make the reader act or imagine
Exclamations show strong emotion and humour
Statements carry the main story
teach.note: Show an all-statement paragraph then a version mixing types. Ask which feels like a person speaking. Tell pupils a preface should sound like a friendly person speaking directly to the reader, but remain respectful and honest.

practice: Label each sentence: (a) ‘Listen carefully.’ (b) ‘My brother snored like a bear!’ (c) ‘Where did the biscuits go?’ (d) ‘We lived by the sea.’
Turn the statement ‘The classroom was silent.’ into a question, a command and an exclamation.
Which type would you use to open a preface to hook a reader, and why?
independent: Write a preface of 5-6 sentences to your own autobiography for readers your age. Use all four sentence types and say what the book will and will not include.
Colour-code your sentence types (use underlines in a document if needed) and check that each type appears at least once.
Extension: add a rhetorical question that makes the reader curious.
exit: Write a command sentence and an exclamation about your favourite place.
Why would a writer open a preface with a question?
lessons.homework: Finish your preface and underline each sentence type in a different colour or style.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a preface frame with one sentence-starter per type. EAL: finger-signal game for types. Stretch: analyse how Dahl's voice differs from a more formal autobiography.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Voice, humour and description (Roald Dahl's Boy)
lessons.title: Dahl and exaggeration: humour, truthfulness and The Great Mouse Plot
objectives: Explain how exaggeration (hyperbole) creates humour
Discuss how reliable memory is in autobiography
Write an exaggerated but respectful description

keywords.def: deliberate exaggeration for effect, e.g. ‘a queue a mile long’
a description that exaggerates features of a person for comic effect
able to be trusted as accurate
the quality of being funny
the attitude or feeling a writer creates

starter: Give an example of each sentence type about the sea.
Which sentence type is ‘Look at that!’?
Why do autobiographies use first person?

teach.heading: The Great Mouse Plot
bullets: Boy: Dahl and friends at school in Llandaff
The boys played a prank on a sweet-shop owner
Dahl tells it with comic detail and suspense
Humour comes from exaggeration
teach.note: Summarise the episode in your own words or read a short extract from the class copy (do not copy long passages onto slides). In brief: as young schoolboys, Dahl and his friends played a trick on a grumpy sweet-shop keeper by placing a dead mouse in a jar of sweets, and then faced the consequences at school. Ask: ‘Is Dahl proud of the prank?’ Note the cheeky narrator's voice. Add that pranks that harm or humiliate people are not in line with our adab.

teach.heading: Hyperbole and caricature
bullets: Hyperbole: ‘a million sweets in the window’
Caricature: enlarge one feature for comic effect
Exaggeration makes small events feel enormous
Check the tone: is it playful or cruel?
teach.note: Give original examples: ‘The queue for the tuck shop stretched to the next town.’ Ask pupils to improve a plain sentence: ‘The teacher was strict.’ Discuss tone. The Qur'an (49:11) warns believers not to mock one another or call each other offensive names, so ask: ‘When does funny become unkind?’ Pupils use caricature of invented characters, not real people.

teach.heading: Can we trust a memory?
bullets: Memory fades and changes over time
Writers may shape stories to entertain
Honest writers do not invent harmful lies
Truthfulness is a Muslim virtue
teach.note: Cite plainly: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask: ‘Is exaggerating for a joke the same as lying?’ Discuss that a reader understands playful exaggeration when the tone makes it clear, but a writer must not deceive. Link to RECIPE Integrity.

teach.heading: Writing comic description
bullets: Choose a character or situation
Use one hyperbole and one simile
Keep the tone playful, never cruel
End with a punchline or reflection
teach.note: Model: ‘Mr Hakim's moustache was so enormous that two sparrows had built a nest in it and paid no rent.’ Invented character, harmless. Ask for improvements. Remind pupils to use specific, concrete detail; vague hyperbole is weak (‘very very big’).

practice: Spot the hyperbole: ‘The homework pile was taller than the school.’ ‘The tea was cold.’ ‘I waited forever for the bus.’ Which one is not hyperbole?
Rewrite using hyperbole: ‘The playground was crowded.’
Is this playful or unkind, and why? ‘Everyone knows Sami is the stupidest boy in the world.’ How could it be rewritten kindly?
independent: Write a 6-8 sentence comic description of an invented shopkeeper, teacher or neighbour, using two hyperboles, one simile and one question.
Add a final sentence explaining honestly what really happened (a reflection or ‘truth’ sentence).
Extension: write two sentences about why an autobiographer might exaggerate and one reason not to.
exit: Define hyperbole and give an original example.
Why must writers be careful when making fun of others?
lessons.homework: Read a chapter extract of Boy (or listen to the author-read extract provided by the teacher) and note three examples of humour.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a hyperbole word bank and picture prompts. EAL: use visual vocabulary for comparing size. Stretch: analyse the difference between exaggeration and untruth.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Voice, humour and description (Roald Dahl's Boy)
lessons.title: Writing from memory: sensory description and noun phrases
objectives: Use the five senses to describe a remembered place
Build noun phrases with pre- and post-modification
Use a simile and a metaphor accurately

keywords.def: words that appeal to sight, sound, smell, taste or touch
a noun with words that describe it, e.g. the creaky wooden gate
describing words placed before the noun
extra detail placed after the noun, e.g. the gate behind the shed
comparing two things using like or as

starter: Give an example of hyperbole about food.
Explain tone in your own words.
Write a command sentence about a memory.

teach.heading: The five senses
bullets: Sight: colours, shapes, movement
Sound: whispers, clatter, hush
Smell: baking, rain, smoke
Touch: rough, silky, scalding
Taste: salty, sour, sweet
teach.note: Say bismillah and reflect on the senses as blessings from Allah. Ask pupils to close their eyes and recall their grandparents' kitchen or a favourite shop; take two words per sense in chat. Note that memory is often triggered by smell. Misconception: description is only about sight.

teach.heading: Noun phrases
bullets: Plain: ‘the kitchen’
Pre-modified: ‘the tiny, steamy kitchen’
Post-modified: ‘the kitchen at the end of the hall’
Both: ‘the tiny, steamy kitchen at the end of the hall’
teach.note: Build the phrase live, one layer at a time. Practice with ‘a bicycle’. Common mistake: stacking adjectives that do not add anything (‘big large huge’). Choose precise adjectives; use commas between adjectives that could be swapped with ‘and’.

teach.heading: Similes and metaphors
bullets: Simile: ‘steam rose like a ghost from the pot’
Metaphor: ‘the pot was a small volcano’
Choose comparisons that fit the mood
Avoid clichés: ‘as white as snow’
teach.note: Explain metaphor says something is something else. Ask: ‘What does a volcano suggest about the pot?’ (danger, heat). Encourage original comparisons rooted in the pupils' own lives. Warning: too many comparisons can overload a paragraph, so aim for one or two.

teach.heading: Model paragraph
bullets: Opens with a place and a sense
Moves around the room, like a camera
Ends with a feeling or reflection
teach.note: Read this teacher model: ‘Nana's kitchen smelled of cardamom and warm bread. A cracked blue teapot hissed on the stove, and the radio murmured in the corner like a sleepy cat. I remember the stickiness of the plastic tablecloth beneath my elbows. Even now, one sniff of cardamom and I am small again.’ Ask pupils to find two senses, a simile and a noun phrase.

practice: Expand into a noun phrase with pre- and post-modification: ‘a bag’, ‘a street’.
Add a simile: ‘The rain fell…’. Add a metaphor: ‘The sun was…’.
Which sense is missing from the model paragraph? Add one sentence to include it.
independent: Write a descriptive paragraph (7-8 sentences) about a place from your childhood. Include at least four senses, three noun phrases and one original simile.
Highlight your noun phrases and mark them ‘pre’ or ‘post’.
Extension: end with a reflection sentence linking the place to who you are now.
exit: Write one noun phrase with both pre- and post-modification.
Write a simile about a sound.
lessons.homework: Draft a sensory description of a place you love (home, masjid, grandparents' house) in 8 sentences. Use one sense per sentence in your first five.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence frames per sense and a word bank. EAL: sensory picture cards to build vocabulary before writing. Stretch: experiment with a short fragment sentence for impact.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Voice, humour and description (Roald Dahl's Boy)
lessons.title: Reading an unseen extract: building our toolkit
objectives: Use a step-by-step method to read an unseen extract
Select short evidence and comment on its effect
Answer an AQA-style question: how does the writer show…?

keywords.def: a text you have not studied before
a short quotation or detail from the text that supports your point
a conclusion based on clues in the text
what the writer makes the reader think or feel
the position from which a story is told

starter: Define simile and metaphor.
What is a noun phrase? Give one.
Name three senses a writer might use.

teach.heading: Our five-step toolkit
bullets: Read once for meaning: who, what, where?
Read again: underline interesting words
Ask: what is the writer trying to make me feel?
Pick short evidence
Explain the effect in detail
teach.note: Say bismillah. Tell pupils this toolkit will be used all year. It prepares them for the AQA GCSE exam style: AO1 (find and interpret ideas) and AO2 (language and structure). Model Step 1 quickly: pupils tell you who is speaking and what is happening in 20 seconds.

teach.heading: Evidence and inference
bullets: Evidence: a short quote, 1-5 words
Inference: what the evidence suggests
Use ‘suggests’, ‘implies’, ‘shows’
Do not retell the text
teach.note: Model: the words ‘my hands trembled’ suggest nerves. Good evidence is short. Misconception: copying a whole sentence. Cut it down to the key word. Ask: ‘What else could trembling suggest?’ (cold, excitement). Accept reasoned alternatives.

teach.heading: Writing about effect
bullets: Word choice: why this word, not another?
What does it make the reader feel?
‘The verb ‘crept’ suggests…’
Zoom in on one word
teach.note: Show a weak and a strong response. Weak: ‘The writer uses a metaphor to make it interesting.’ Strong: ‘The metaphor ‘a locked gate’ suggests the narrator feels shut out, which makes the reader sympathise.’ Teach a sentence stem: The word … suggests … which makes the reader feel …

teach.heading: Model question
bullets: Q: How does the writer show the narrator's nerves?
Find 2-3 pieces of evidence
Explain each in a full sentence
Write 3-4 sentences
teach.note: The unseen extract is in the practice section. Read it aloud, then model Steps 1 to 3 together. Pupils then complete the answer in guided practice. Remind them of the success criteria: point, short evidence, explanation of effect.

practice: Read the teacher-written extract: ‘The corridor to the headteacher's office stretched ahead of me like a tunnel. My shoes squeaked on the polished floor, each step louder than the last. I tucked my shaking hands into my pockets and told myself it was only a conversation. The door was open a crack; a murmur of voices drifted out. I swallowed hard, lifted my hand, and froze.’ Step 1: who is speaking, and where are they?
Underline three words or phrases that show nerves. Pick the best one and explain its effect.
Complete the stem: The phrase ‘squeaked on the polished floor’ suggests…
independent: Answer in 4 sentences: How does the writer show that the narrator is nervous? Use two pieces of short evidence.
Swap answers with a partner. Tick evidence that is short; star any sentence that explains effect.
Extension: write one sentence on how the sentence structure of the last line creates tension.
exit: List the five steps of our toolkit.
Write one stem sentence explaining the effect of a single word.
lessons.homework: Write a paragraph answering: How does the writer of the extract make the corridor seem frightening? Use two short quotations.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a highlighted extract and an evidence grid. EAL: pre-teach ‘tunnel’, ‘murmur’, ‘froze’. Stretch: compare the extract with Dahl's comic tone.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Writing our own autobiographical episode
lessons.title: Planning an autobiographical episode: structure and reflection
objectives: Choose a significant moment and plan its structure
Write an engaging opening that hooks the reader
Include reflection that shows what the moment meant

keywords.def: an opening that grabs the reader's attention
the most tense or important moment in a story
how the situation is settled at the end
the writer's thoughts about what an event meant
the shape of a story from beginning to end

starter: How do you find evidence in an unseen text?
Complete: The word ‘froze’ suggests…
Give an example of a time adverbial.

teach.heading: Choosing the moment
bullets: Small moments can be powerful
Choose one event, not a whole year
Pick something with feelings and a lesson
Keep private matters private
teach.note: Say bismillah. Discuss that autobiographers choose carefully. Pupils should never share anything that makes them or others uncomfortable or unsafe; the teacher offers safe topics (first day at a new school, learning to ride a bike, a family trip, a Ramadan memory, a day something went wrong). If any pupil appears to hint at a worry, follow the TGA Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy and speak to the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: A shape for the episode
bullets: Hook: a surprising first line
Build-up: set the scene and the feeling
Climax: the key moment
Aftermath: what happened next
Reflection: what it taught you
teach.note: Show the arc visually as a mountain. Use the ‘bicycle off the jetty’ model: hook (the wheels in the air), build-up (setting off), climax (the splash), aftermath (laughter), reflection (laughing at myself). Misconception: that there must be a dramatic event. Quiet moments can have a strong arc.

teach.heading: Hooks that work
bullets: A sound: ‘Crash!’
A question to the reader
A bold statement: ‘I should never have…’
Dialogue in the middle of action
teach.note: Give four openings for the same episode and vote on the best. Discuss why ‘One day I went to the park’ is weak. Model improving it: ‘The swing creaked once, twice, and then I was flying.’ Ask pupils to produce a hook in 60 seconds and share in chat.

teach.heading: Making reflection meaningful
bullets: Say what you felt then and now
Show what you learned or how you changed
Avoid ‘and I learned never to do it again’
Keep reflection to 2-3 sentences
teach.note: Model weak versus strong reflection. Weak: ‘It was a good day.’ Strong: ‘I thought being brave meant not being scared; now I know it means going on anyway.’ Link to RECIPE Resilience: the Qur'an reminds us that with hardship comes ease (94:5-6).

practice: Fill in the arc planning grid for ‘My first day at a new school’: hook / build-up / climax / aftermath / reflection. Use real details.
Improve this weak opening: ‘It was a sunny day and I went to the beach.’ Write two better hooks.
Write a reflection sentence starting ‘At the time I thought…, but now I know…’.
independent: Complete your own planning grid for an episode that you choose. Write all five boxes in note form.
Write your hook and your first paragraph (4-5 sentences), using a time adverbial and one sensory detail.
Extension: plan where you could add a flashback.
exit: What are the five parts of our narrative arc?
Write a hook for an episode about a time you were lost.
lessons.homework: Complete your plan and draft the build-up paragraph (5-6 sentences) of your episode.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a pre-filled arc template with sentence starters. EAL: allow bilingual planning notes. Stretch: use two time frames, past and present.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Writing our own autobiographical episode
lessons.title: Drafting, editing and sharing: SPaG and peer feedback
objectives: Complete a draft of an autobiographical episode
Proofread for tense, punctuation and sentence variety
Give and respond to kind, specific feedback

keywords.def: to check writing carefully for errors
keeping verbs in the same tense unless there is a reason to change
a mark showing missing letters (don't) or possession (Amir's)
a word or phrase at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma
comments that help improve work

starter: Name the five parts of a narrative arc.
Write a hook sentence using a sound.
Why is reflection important in autobiography?

teach.heading: The editing mindset
bullets: First drafts are for ideas
Second drafts are for improvement
Read aloud to catch mistakes
Edit with a purpose: one focus at a time
teach.note: Say bismillah. Link editing to Excellence (ihsan): doing our work as well as we can. Model reading aloud to hear missing words. Misconception: that proofreading means only spelling. Show the five checks on the next slide.

teach.heading: Five checks
bullets: Tense: past throughout, unless reflecting
Capital letters and full stops
Apostrophes: don't, Amir's
Commas after fronted adverbials and in lists
Variety: at least one question or exclamation
teach.note: Display this faulty sentence: ‘Last summer i go to my grandmas house, we played in the garden and then it was raining.’ Ask pupils to correct together (tense, capital I, apostrophe, comma splice). Check comma use and sentence boundaries. Common error: comma splice.

teach.heading: Proofread a model
bullets: Find the tense slips
Find missing apostrophes
Fix one run-on sentence
Improve one weak word
teach.note: Use the faulty paragraph from the practice questions. Pupils type corrections into chat or hold up numbers. Keep it brisk. Praise accuracy and explain each correction in a sentence. Encourage the language of grammar: ‘This verb is in present tense but the story is in past’.

teach.heading: Giving kind feedback
bullets: WWW: what went well
EBI: even better if
Be specific: quote the line
Be kind, true and helpful
teach.note: Link to adab: advising a brother or sister sincerely is part of our deen, but we do it gently. Model a good comment: ‘Your simile about the kettle sounding like a train was vivid. Even better if you check the tense in paragraph 2.’ Pair pupils for a short peer review in breakout rooms or by sharing a document.

practice: Correct: ‘Last summer i go to my grandmas house. We playd in the garden, and then it start raining so we goes inside.’ Rewrite in full.
Add a fronted adverbial with a comma to: ‘We ate the cake.’ Then add a question sentence.
Write one WWW and one EBI for this extract: ‘The kettle screamed like a train. We ran in. Mum is smiling.’
independent: Finish your autobiographical episode (200-250 words) using your plan. Include a hook, at least three senses, one simile and a reflection.
Proofread using the five checks. Mark each check with a tick.
Share a paragraph with a partner and write one WWW and one EBI for each other.
exit: Which of the five checks did you find most useful, and why?
